transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. Um, I hope I'm not wasting your time with this, but... I guess I've been struggling a bit at work. 

I'm a high school teacher, and, well, I know everyone gets tired, right? So it might just be normal stress. But lately, I'll sit down with a stack of essays or a curriculum document, fully intending to get to work—and I really do try—but within ten minutes or so, I’ll realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page. My mind will have wandered off, and I'll be thinking about three other things, barely taking in what’s right in front of me. 

It's a bit embarrassing to admit, honestly, because I feel like I should just be able to push through and do my job. Does that make sense? Is that the kind of thing you usually help people with?
Over the past few weeks, aside from the difficulty concentrating at work, have you noticed changes in your mood—like feeling down, sad, or empty for most of the day?

Oh, um... no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. I definitely get a little frustrated with myself when I can't finish my grading, but... no, I wouldn't say I feel sad or empty. 

I actually feel pretty okay most of the time, mood-wise, you know? I have a really good life, so I'd feel terrible complaining about being sad when I'm really not. I hope that's okay? Like, I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information. But yeah, no real sadness... just that annoyance at myself for being so scattered. Is that a normal way to feel?
When you're trying to focus on work, do you also feel restless or fidgety—like you need to get up and move around, or do things feel kind of slow and sluggish instead?

Um, actually, no, I don't really get that urge to get up and move around. I can sit still just fine, thankfully. I guess I'd be a pretty terrible teacher if I couldn't even sit at my desk, right? 

And I wouldn't say I feel sluggish, either. It's more just... my body is right there, completely still, but my brain is just miles away. I'm not physically restless at all. 

I hope I'm answering that right? Like, I don't want to mislead you or leave anything out. But yeah, no real fidgeting or feeling slow. Just the zoning out. Does that... does that still make sense for what we're talking about?

How long have you been experiencing this difficulty concentrating? Has this been something you've struggled with since childhood, or is this more of a recent problem that started within the last few weeks or months?

Well, I guess... I mean, I've always been a little bit of a daydreamer, even when I was a kid. But it was never really a *problem*, you know? I always managed to get good grades and everything, so I don't want to make it sound like I was struggling back then. 

But as far as it being an actual issue... I'd say it's been noticeably worse for about, um, maybe 11 months now? Yeah, almost a year. The school changed our whole curriculum calendar around then, and they added all these mandatory after-school planning meetings. 

I really want to do a good job with all the new requirements, but since all that started, it's just been so much harder to keep my head in the game. I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just making excuses or complaining about the extra work! I know everyone else is dealing with the same changes. But that's really when I started noticing that I couldn't just power through the zoning out anymore. Is it normal for things to kind of... flare up like that when your schedule changes?

In the past year or so, have you had any significant medical events—like an infection, head injury, surgery, or major illness? Or have you started any new medications or supplements around the time your concentration problems began?

Oh, um, let me think... no. No, I haven't had anything like that. I'm actually pretty healthy, thankfully. I try to take good care of myself so I don't have to call out sick too often—the kids really need consistency, you know? So, no surgeries or head injuries or major illnesses at all. 

And as for medications, no, I don't take anything. Well, I mean, I take a standard multivitamin sometimes when I remember, but I don't think that counts, right? I definitely haven't started any new supplements or anything around the time my focus got worse. 

I hope that's a good thing? Like, maybe it helps rule some of the scarier stuff out for you? I just want to make sure I'm giving you all the right pieces to the puzzle.
Have you noticed any other physical symptoms over the past year—like headaches, memory problems beyond just concentration, difficulty with balance, or anything else unusual with your health?

Um, no, nothing like that. I haven't had any headaches or balance issues or anything. My health has been really steady, which I'm super grateful for. 

And my memory is... well, it's fine! I mean, sure, I might forget where I put my keys every now and then, or forget to grab a copy from the printer, but that's just normal, right? Nothing major. I definitely remember all my students' names and my lesson plans and all the important stuff. 

So yeah, no other physical symptoms at all. Just the trouble staying focused. I really hope I'm being helpful here. I know it must be frustrating when a patient doesn't have a lot of clear-cut physical signs for you to look at. Am I giving you what you need to figure this out?
Over this past year, have you felt emotionally exhausted or burned out—like you're running on empty, or that your emotional reserves are just depleted—even when you're not physically tired?

Um, well... no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, teaching is definitely a demanding job, especially with all those new meetings, but I really love what I do. I love being there for the kids. So I don't feel... burned out or emotionally depleted, you know? I definitely don't want to sound like I'm unhappy with my career or complaining about the students, because I'm not. 

I still really care about the work, and I feel like I have the emotional energy for it... it's just the actual focusing part that's tripping me up. Like, my heart is totally in it, but my brain just keeps wandering off when I need to sit down and plan. 

I hope that makes sense? I know a lot of people get burned out in education, and it's totally understandable, but I try really hard to keep a positive attitude and just push through. Does that help narrow things down for you? I just want to make sure I'm being a good historian for you and giving you the right kind of information.

Have you ever had any neurological conditions like migraines, seizures, thyroid problems, or sleep disorders? And how is your sleep been over this past year—are you getting enough sleep and feeling rested when you wake up?

Um, no, no neurological conditions. I've never had a seizure or a migraine, and my thyroid has always been fine whenever they've checked it at my regular physicals. And no sleep disorders either. 

My sleep is... it's really good, actually. I mean, I try to get my eight hours every night. Sometimes I might stay up a little late grading papers, but I always make sure I get enough rest so I can be present for the students the next day. I wake up feeling fine, you know? Ready to go. 

So, yeah, sleep is definitely not an issue. I know lack of sleep can make it hard to concentrate, so I've been really careful about keeping a good schedule. I hope that's helpful? I'm trying to make sure I'm doing all the right things on my end, so if my sleep is good, maybe that helps you figure out what's actually going wrong with my focus?
Have you had any recent blood work or lab tests done—like checking your blood sugar, vitamin levels, or hormone levels? And if so, were all the results normal?

Um, let's see... no, I haven't had any new blood work done recently. Just my standard annual physical a while back, and my primary doctor said everything looked great. Blood sugar, vitamins, all of that was completely normal. I always make sure to go to my yearly checkups, so I try to stay really on top of my health. 

But I haven't had any special labs drawn lately. Is that... is that something I should have done before coming in today? I can totally call my regular doctor and get some tests scheduled if you need those numbers to rule things out. I really don't mind doing that at all! I just want to make sure you have everything you need from me to figure this out. Should I go ahead and try to get that set up for you?
Has your primary care doctor or anyone else ordered any brain imaging—like an MRI or CT scan—or done any formal cognitive testing to evaluate your concentration problems?

Um, no, no brain imaging or anything like that. No MRI or CT scans. And no formal cognitive testing either. 

I guess my primary doctor didn't really think it was necessary? When I mentioned the focus stuff, they just suggested I come talk to someone like you who specializes in it. I hope that's okay! I mean, I can absolutely ask them for a referral for a scan if you think it's important. I just assumed since I haven't had any head injuries or anything, it probably wasn't a brain thing... like, a structural brain thing, you know? 

But I'm totally open to doing whatever testing you think would be helpful. I really just want to follow your lead on this. Does it make sense that we haven't done any of those tests yet, or did I drop the ball by not asking my regular doctor for them first?

Besides the curriculum changes at school about 11 months ago, have there been any other major life changes or stressful events around that same time—like changes in your personal relationships, family situations, living situation, or anything else significant happening in your life?

Um, no, no other major changes. Just the curriculum overhaul at work, which was... well, it was a lot, but I've been really trying my best to stay on top of it. 

As for everything else, things have been pretty stable. My relationships are good, my family is doing well, and I haven't moved or anything like that. I try to keep my personal life pretty organized and drama-free so I can focus on my students. I know stress can really mess with your concentration, so I've been doing my best to keep everything else running smoothly. 

I hope it's okay that there isn't really anything else going on? I know sometimes it's easier to pinpoint a problem when there's a clear cause, like a big life event. But honestly, everything outside of school has been completely normal. I'm really trying to give you all the pieces here, so I hope I'm not leaving anything out that you might need?

I'd like to go back to something—around the time your concentration problems started 11 months ago, did you experience any viral infections, illnesses like COVID, or anything that made you feel physically unwell, even if it seemed minor at the time?

Um, no... no, I didn't have anything like that. No COVID, no flu, or any weird viral stuff around that time. I'm usually pretty healthy, honestly. 

I mean, working in a school, you're always around kids with the sniffles, so I'm really careful about washing my hands and staying on top of my immune system. I try to be really responsible about that so I don't miss work or get anyone else sick. But yeah, nothing stands out as being physically unwell right when all this started. 

Is it... is it common for an illness to cause focus issues like this? I hope I'm not missing some obvious connection. I really want to make sure I'm giving you the right information. Do you think I should have paid closer attention to minor colds back then?
Looking back over your lifetime, have you ever had a serious head injury or concussion—even if it was years ago and seemed fine at the time—or any kind of brain infection or encephalitis?

Um, no, no serious head injuries or anything like that. I've never had a concussion, and definitely no brain infections either. I've always been pretty careful, you know? Just... playing it safe. 

I mean, I've bumped my head on a cabinet door or something minor like anyone else, but never anything where I blacked out or needed to see a doctor. I really hope that's the kind of answer you're looking for? I just want to make sure I'm not missing some tiny detail from when I was a kid that you might need for your assessment. Am I doing okay with these questions? I really want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need to figure this out.

When you're trying to focus on your work, do you also notice difficulty finding the right words when you're speaking, or trouble organizing your thoughts into a clear plan—or does it feel more like your mind is just wandering away from something you could otherwise do fine?

Um, no, I wouldn't say I have trouble finding words or... or organizing my thoughts, really. I mean, as a teacher, I have to be pretty good at explaining things, so I feel like my communication is usually pretty solid. 

It's really just... it's more like my mind just kind of drifts off. Like, I know exactly what I need to do, and I have a good plan for it, but then I'll be reading an assignment or trying to grade a paper, and suddenly I'm just thinking about something else entirely. It's not that I can't do the work—I really can, and I always try my best to get it done right! It's just that staying locked onto it is... harder than it should be, I guess? 

I hope that makes sense? I don't want to make it sound like I can't think clearly or do my job, because I really do care about my work. Is that the kind of distinction you were asking about? I just want to make sure I'm answering this the right way for you.

In the months after that curriculum change started, did you notice any other symptoms that seemed unusual or off—like brain fog, unusual fatigue, or feeling like you were recovering from something, even if you weren't sure what it was?

Um, no, I really didn't notice anything like that. No brain fog or feeling like I was getting over a sickness or anything. 

I mean, obviously, teaching can leave you a little tired by the end of the week, especially when you're trying to adapt to a whole new curriculum, but it was just normal tiredness, I promise. Not like an unusual fatigue. I always try to keep my energy up for the kids, you know? I wouldn't want to let them down by dragging through the day, so I made sure to stay on top of things physically. 

So, yeah, I felt totally fine in that regard. It was really just... just the wandering mind stuff when I sat down to do the actual desk work. I hope that's helpful? I'm trying really hard to think back and be thorough, but I definitely don't want to claim I had symptoms that weren't there. Am I answering these the right way for you? I just want to make sure I'm giving you a clear picture.
When the curriculum changes started 11 months ago, did your concentration problems begin right away—like within days or a week or two—or did they develop more gradually over several weeks after that?

Um, well, it was... I'd say it was pretty noticeable right around that time, yeah. Like, maybe not the very first day, but definitely within that first week or two. 

It's been about 11 months now since they changed the curriculum calendar and, um, they also added these after-school planning meetings. And I really want to be a team player, you know? I don't want to complain about the extra meetings because I know everyone is working hard to make the new curriculum successful. But it was right around then that I really started noticing the... the difficulty staying focused on the grading and the lesson plans. 

I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just making excuses because of the new schedule? I really do try to stay on top of everything, and I feel bad that I've been struggling with it. I just... I want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline. Does that sound like what you were asking? I want to make sure I'm being helpful.

When you mentioned your concentration problems to your primary care doctor, did they do any testing or evaluation to try to figure out what might be causing the focus issues, or did they just refer you to me without investigating further?

Um, they didn't really do any testing, no. I mean, I brought it up at my check-up because I was just feeling so... behind on everything, and I guess I just wanted to make sure there wasn't something physically wrong with me. 

But my doctor just listened to me describe what was going on with the grading and the meetings, and then they just suggested I talk to someone like you who specializes in this kind of thing. They didn't run any blood tests or anything like that. I hope that's okay? I didn't want to push them to do tests if they didn't think it was necessary, because I trust their judgment, you know? 

I just... I want to make sure I'm doing everything I'm supposed to be doing to figure this out. Should I have asked them to do some kind of evaluation first? I really hope I didn't skip a step before coming to see you.

In that first week or two after the curriculum changes started, do you remember if you had even a mild cold, sore throat, or any kind of infection—something that lasted just a few days—even if you didn't think it was serious enough to mention before?

Um, no, I really don't think so. I'm pretty sure I didn't have a cold or a sore throat or anything like that. 

I mean, I'm usually pretty good about washing my hands and using hand sanitizer, especially being around high schoolers all day. You kind of have to be, right? So I didn't have any kind of bug or infection that I can remember. I felt totally fine physically, just... just overwhelmed by the new schedule and the paperwork. 

I really hope I'm not missing something important that you need to know. I'm trying my best to remember every little detail from back then. Is it okay that I didn't have a cold? I just want to make sure I'm giving you all the right pieces of the puzzle.

Has your primary care doctor ever mentioned anything about your thyroid function, blood pressure, or any other medical condition—even something they said was minor or didn't need treatment—that might have developed or changed around the time your focus problems started?

Um, no, my doctor hasn't mentioned anything like that. My blood pressure is usually pretty good, I think? And they've never brought up my thyroid or anything else being off. 

I mean, I'm pretty healthy overall, which I'm really grateful for. I go to my yearly physicals and try to take care of myself so I can keep up with the kids at school. So, yeah, no new medical issues or anything that changed around that time. 

I hope that's a good thing? I mean, I know it would be easier if there was just a simple blood test that explained everything, but I promise I'm not hiding any medical conditions from you. I just... I really want to be completely honest so you can help me figure this out. Does that all make sense?

Looking back to around 11 months ago when the curriculum changes started, did your primary care doctor ever check your blood work or run any tests at that time, or even mention any concerns about your health—even if they said everything was fine?

Um, no, they didn't run any blood work or do any tests back then either. I didn't actually go to the doctor right when all the curriculum stuff started. I just... I figured it was just normal stress from work, you know? So I didn't think I needed to bother my doctor about it at the time.

I hope it was okay that I waited to go in until my regular check-up? I really try not to be one of those people who goes to the doctor for every little thing, so I just tried to push through it. But no, they haven't mentioned any health concerns at all over the last year. I hope I'm answering this the way you need me to? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent difficulty concentrating that began 11 months ago following workplace stress (curriculum changes and increased meetings). Key features support Neurasthenia (F48.0): (1) Onset clearly linked to psychosocial stressor (work reorganization); (2) Primary complaint is mental fatigue/difficulty sustaining attention rather than mood symptoms; (3) No evidence of mood disorder (explicitly denies sadness, emptiness, or emotional depletion); (4) No physical restlessness or psychomotor changes; (5) Comprehensive medical workup ruled out organic causes (no head injury, infection, neurological conditions, abnormal labs, medication effects); (6) Functional impairment present (difficulty completing work tasks); (7) No evidence of structural brain pathology or post-infectious syndrome. F06.8 (Other specified mental disorder due to known physiological condition) is less likely given the thorough exclusion of medical/neurological etiologies and absence of acute infection or illness around symptom onset.
